sections.heading: The place
paragraphs: St. Maries is a working logging town on the St. Joe River in northern Idaho. The river made the town, and the river is famous: the U.S. Forest Service calls the lower St. Joe the highest navigable river in the world. River writers add an honest footnote — “by some definitions.”
A hundred years ago, paddle-wheel steamboats carried as many as 1,000 passengers up this river. The steamboats are gone. The work isn't: tugboats still tow rafts of logs past town, down to the mills.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: In August 1910, the fire everyone here just calls the 1910 fire tore through these mountains. Firefighters died across the region, and dozens of them were brought to St. Maries and buried together at Woodlawn Cemetery, west of town.

They lie in circles around a granite marker shaped like a flame, put up by the Forest Service, and the town has kept the memorial ever since. The books don't quite agree on the count — 54 to 59 men, depending on the source — so this page prints the range instead of pretending.

bullets: Woodlawn Cemetery — the circles of firefighters' graves and the flame-shaped marker, west of town.
The riverfront — tugs towing log rafts still pass. There's no schedule; stand on the bank a while and watch the river work.
Logger's Memorial Park, downtown — a memorial naming more than 250 St. Joe loggers killed on the job.
Hughes House Museum, at Sixth and Main — a historic log house that holds the town's logging history.
The St. Joe River Scenic Byway — 47 miles upriver to Avery, through the country the log drives came down.
sections.heading: What you can see now

bullets: St. Maries has full services year-round. Local time is Pacific.
Woodlawn Cemetery is public ground in daylight. It is a working cemetery — go on the paths, and visit like a guest.
The byway is open to Avery all year. Past Avery the road isn't plowed and can be snowed shut, roughly November to May.
Hughes House hours weren't verified for this page — check before you count on it being open.
sections.heading: Before you go
The place
paragraphs: Just south of Wallace, Idaho, a trail climbs the West Fork of Placer Creek: two miles each way on Trail No. 38, the Pulaski Tunnel Trail. At the end of it, across the creek, is a hole in the ground — the Nicholson adit, an old prospect tunnel where no ore was ever found.
The trailhead sign lays out the whole canyon story — the map, the creek, the route — before you walk it.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: On August 20, 1910, the Big Burn — the fire that burned about three million acres across northern Idaho, western Montana, and eastern Washington — drove ranger Ed Pulaski up this canyon with the men he could gather. Pulaski knew the old tunnel and got his crew of 45 inside.

He held the entrance through the night, and at five in the morning forty people walked out. Five of the crew died in the tunnel and one man was killed on the way in. The books differ a little on the count, and the full record below prints the difference honestly instead of smoothing it over.

sections.heading: What you can see now
bullets: The trailhead interpretive sign and map — the whole canyon story in one panel.
The adit portal itself, viewed from the overlook across the creek at the trail's end.
The escape-route ground along the West Fork of Placer Creek, two miles each way.
The trail bridge whose posts carry Pulaski tools — the tool Pulaski himself designed.

sections.heading: Before you go
bullets: The walk is two miles each way from the trailhead just south of Wallace.
You view the tunnel from the overlook across the creek — the overlook is the visit.
Hours and fees for the trailhead aren't in the record behind this page — check locally before you count on services.

sections.heading: The place
paragraphs: Wallace is a small mining town in a steep northern Idaho canyon, and its whole downtown is the site: block after block of 1890s brick, with the freeway passing overhead on stilts. The entire downtown is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: Wallace's wooden downtown burned in 1890, and the town rebuilt in brick, stone, and steel. Twenty years later, on August 20, 1910, the Big Burn came down out of the forests. That afternoon a warm fog lay so thick the streetlights came on at 3 p.m.; people buried their possessions in their yards, and women and children were put on trains out of town.
The fire took about a third of Wallace, mostly the east side. The brick core, built after 1890 for exactly that day, largely held — and it is the downtown you walk today.

sections.heading: What you can see now
bullets: Bank Street and Cedar Street — the post-1890 brick rebuild that faced the 1910 fire.
The Northern Pacific Depot (1901–02), now the depot museum — the railroad that evacuated the town.
The Shoshone County Courthouse (1907), which stood through the fire.
The Carnegie Library (1910–11), rising the year after the burn.
The east end of town — the ground the 1910 fire actually took, read against the brick core it couldn't.

sections.heading: Before you go
bullets: Start at the Northern Pacific Depot Museum and walk the brick blocks — the whole downtown is the site.
The depot museum's hours aren't in the record behind this page — check before you count on it being open.

sections.heading: The place
paragraphs: Burke is a ghost town seven miles up a canyon from Wallace — a canyon so narrow, about 300 feet at its tightest, that the town, the creek, the road, and the railroad all had to share the same ground.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: Lead-silver-zinc was found in Burke Canyon in 1884, and the town was established in 1887. The canyon set the terms for everything: buildings went up over the creek and over the railroad, shops pulled in their awnings when trains passed, and the main street was the railroad.

The 150-room Tiger Hotel, built in 1896, was rebuilt so the Northern Pacific ran straight through its lobby — five trains a day in its heyday, by the hotel-era accounts. Mining faded across the last century, the last mine closed in 1991, and the record puts the population at about 15.

sections.heading: What you can see now
bullets: The canyon itself — stand on Burke's single street and measure the 300 feet with your eyes.
The mill and mine ruins along the canyon, and surviving brick storefronts.
The Tiger Hotel ground on main street — the hotel is gone, but the street, the creek, and the rail grade still run through where its lobby stood.

sections.heading: Before you go
bullets: Burke is a lived-in ghost town with private property among the ruins — view from the public street, respect postings, and do not enter structures.
Hours, fees, and parking aren't in the record behind this page — the street is the viewpoint.

sections.heading: The place
paragraphs: Just off Interstate 90 near Kellogg, at the mouth of Big Creek Canyon, stands a 13-foot miner with his drill raised to the sky — standing on a boulder that carries a plaque of 91 names.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: On the morning of May 2, 1972, 173 men were underground at the Sunshine Mine, one of the nation's premier silver mines, when fire broke out on the air-intake side. The ventilation carried smoke and carbon monoxide through the workings instead of fresh air.

Eighty men got out in the first hours, many hoisted by a hoistman who stayed at his post until the gases took him. Two more were found alive after 175 hours in the dark. Ninety-one men died — the worst mining disaster in Idaho history. The record below prints the places where its own numbers disagree.

sections.heading: What you can see now
bullets: The memorial itself — Ken Lonn's 13-foot miner, sculpted by a former Sunshine miner.
The names plaque on the boulder: 91 names, and a poem by former Governor Phil Batt.
Big Creek Canyon rising behind the memorial — the ground the mine worked.
On May 2 each year — Miners Memorial Day — the valley gathers here, sets out 91 chairs with a lit lamp on each, and turns the lamps off one by one.

sections.heading: Before you go
bullets: It's a roadside memorial — park clear of the highway.
The mine itself is closed and private. The memorial is the visit.

sections.heading: The place
paragraphs: Nine Mile Cemetery sits outside Wallace, Idaho. Among its graves stand two cobblestone monuments to five men who died in a mine tunnel during the Big Burn of 1910.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: The five men who died in Ed Pulaski's tunnel were carried out on packhorses and buried here: an unidentified man, William Learmouth, Richard Woods, Joe Ferro, and August Berger.

Their graves went unmarked for over a decade. Pulaski pressed the Forest Service for twelve years to mark them properly; in 1921 Congress awarded $500, and the two cobblestone monuments went up. The care came from the man; the institution followed afterward, at its own pace.

sections.heading: What you can see now
bullets: The two cobblestone monuments, with the five names from the tunnel.
Wallace below its forested canyon walls — the ground the survivors staggered into over burning logs.

sections.heading: Before you go
bullets: Pair it with the Pulaski Tunnel Trail the same day — the trail in the morning, the names in the afternoon.
Hours for the cemetery aren't in the record behind this page.

sections.heading: The place
paragraphs: Bovill is a small town in Latah County, in the white pine country of northern Idaho. It was never a mill town — it was the junction town that moved the logs out of some of the finest white pine stands in the region. The town counted 191 people in 2020.

sections.heading: What happened here
paragraphs: The town is named for Hugh Bovill, who built a hotel there in 1899. The railroad arrived in 1906, and logging crews shipped out of Bovill to camps in every direction — more than from any town around, by the town historian's account. Potlatch wintered some 260 draft horses, none under a ton, across the meadow from the depot.

The prime cut near town was finished by about 1930. The town's memory is unusually well kept: more than three hundred interviews with the logging generation were recorded in the 1970s and are now digitized at the University of Idaho.

sections.heading: What you can see now
bullets: Main street — stand where the historic photo on this page was taken: the First State Bank corner and the Spokane Hotel block. The photo shows the street before the fire of July 1914 rebuilt it.
The old rail beds and spur-line grades in and around town — the network that moved the logs.
Village Park, and Caroline Park's brick-and-cobblestone 'Billy Walk'.

sections.heading: Before you go
bullets: Pair Bovill with Elk River the same day — the junction and the mill town read as one story.
Hold the historic photo up against the street as it stands — it shows the street before the 1914 fire, not the street today.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: The White Mountain Apache Tribe chartered the Fort Apache Heritage Foundation in 1998. When management of the old fort transferred from the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 2007, the community gained a say in what the buildings would become.

In 2021, Tribal Chairwoman Gwendena Lee-Gatewood described the need for a place where people could commemorate their own history. Later listening sessions brought questions about language and community life into the work of preserving the fort.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The permanent exhibits at Nohwike’ Bágowa Museum tell White Mountain Apache history.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: On July 12, 1917, vigilantes expelled striking copper workers and other residents from Bisbee. One of them was Fred Watson, a tool nipper. After he was driven out, the woman he would marry brought him a suitcase of his clothes.

Sixty years later, Watson remembered what the people who stayed behind had gone through, too. “I'll forget it when I die!” he told interviewer Robert Houston. His account gives a worker’s answer to the museum’s story about how copper built a town.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The museum’s Urban Outpost exhibition tells the community story. The suitcase survives in Watson’s account. The record does not place it in a display case.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Anna Ochoa O’Leary grew up in Clifton, where her father worked for Phelps Dodge. As a spokesperson for a workers’ auxiliary, she wrote letters and statements, traveled and did outreach. Her account shows how much of the town’s labor organizing happened away from the mine.
In her 2023 interview with Jennifer Nájera, O’Leary also remembered disagreement at home. She and her husband did not remember everything the same way.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The museum occupies Eagle Hall. Its original form and detailing survive from the building Antonio and Ambrose Spezia are credited with in 1913.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Marilou Schultz learned to weave from her mother, Martha Gorman Schultz. Weaving helped pay for her education. In her account, the pleasure was also in the challenge of making something of her own.

Textiles have often been known by the trading post that sold them. The Heard Museum’s Twilight exhibition puts makers’ names back beside that story, including Diné artists Calvin Toney and Florence Riggs.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: Twilight is listed in the Virginia G. Piper Grand Gallery through August 1, 2027. The Heard also catalogs Schultz’s 2013 wearing blanket, but its gallery location is unconfirmed.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: As a boy in the Douglas area, Raúl Hector Castro watched other children ride to school while he walked. His family’s livelihood changed after his father, a smelter worker, died. His mother supported the children through her work as a midwife.
Castro told this story to Pam Stevenson in 2013. His question about the trip to school puts the town’s unequal treatment of children into the distance one child had to walk.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Douglas Historical Society runs the museum in the historic Douglas-Williams House.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: When Lowell Observatory employed Elizabeth Langdon Williams in 1905, “computer” was a person’s job. She did calculations in Boston before moving to Flagstaff in April 1919, where she continued calculating and writing letters.

The observatory’s archive says that after Williams married her colleague George Hall Hamilton in 1922, Constance Lowell asked them both to leave. A letter Williams wrote to Percival Lowell in 1910 survives in the archive from her Boston years.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: In his 2022 testimony to the Senate, Havasupai Chairman Thomas Siyuja Sr. described water as essential to life in the Canyon. His account gives the South Rim view a different meaning. Visitors can look into a place that generations of Havasupai people have called home.
Rex Tilousi brought that history to visitors as a Grand Canyon cultural-interpreter ranger beginning in 1998. A Tribal Council remembrance records his work.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The South Rim visitor center lists the 24-minute film We Are Grand Canyon. It brings several communities’ voices together.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: The Wigwam Motel in Holbrook survived because a family chose to reopen it. The motel’s own history names Chester Lewis’s children Clifton, Paul and Elinor among the people who restored it.

In a published interview, Clifton Lewis said visitors’ gratitude for the preservation was a chief reason for opening again. His account records a family decision. The people who cleaned the rooms and kept the business running are harder to find in the surviving record.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The county historical museum occupies the old Holbrook courthouse.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: In March 2015, digitized H. R. Voth photographs were presented to the Hopi Cultural Preservation Office. Hopi Tutuveni reported the presentation to Leigh Kuwanwisiwma and named archivist Stewart Koiyayumptewa for helping arrange it.

Who should see a photograph is part of its history. The office describes the roles of villages, clans and religious societies in protecting knowledge. Readers can follow the handover in the Tribe’s newspaper.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Mary (Shea) Lyons left two interviews about Jerome. One catalog entry follows her years in town from 1925 to 1953. Another lists schools, the library and social life among its subjects.

A teacher’s record asks a different question of a mining town. Where did families learn, read and find company when the working day ended? The catalog identifies those subjects without putting an invented classroom story into Lyons’s mouth.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Mine Museum describes dishes, milk bottles and newspapers among its community displays. No object has been traced to Lyons herself.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: In a 2013 interview, Marshall Trimble told the story of his family’s arrival in 1918. An offer to pick cotton in Mesa came with a tent. Taking the job settled where the family would sleep as well as where they would work.

Trimble was born in 1939. This detail survives because a grandson repeated the story his family had passed down. It tells us about their arrangement without making it the story of every cotton worker.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The museum occupies the Old Lehi School. Its displays rotate, and the record identifies no Trimble family exhibit.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: When Calvin C. Goode wanted to continue mechanical drawing, his segregated school had no course for him. He recalled that a shop teacher formed a class of one. Goode graduated in 1945 and later returned as the school accountant.

Lincoln Ragsdale Jr. remembered a different kind of work in Phoenix. He helped with transport in the family mortuary business and eventually managed it, even though he wanted a different career. The two accounts show what a teacher and a family business made possible, person by person.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Diana Hinojosa DeLugan remembered her father, musician Fidencio Garcia Hinojosa, in a Phoenix household where musical families visited and the family studied for citizenship. Her childhood stories come from the Las Milpas community.
A university article preserved her memories in 2017. Hearing the music and the lessons together in her account gives a sense of how the family lived across two cultures.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: In October 1912, Phoenix Mayor Lloyd Christy gave permission for a Votes for Women banner. On November 5, Arizona voters approved the suffrage initiative.

Eleven days after the vote, organizer Frances Willard Munds urged women to study the laws that governed women and children. The university’s excerpts from the Tucson Citizen preserve her idea of what the work of citizenship would be after election day.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: At Poston, Mas Hashimoto’s mother worked as an assistant cook. In his 2008 interview he remembered her pay as sixteen dollars a month. Even in confinement, the family still owed property taxes elsewhere, and his brothers sent money back.

He also remembered women teaching one another to sew and making their rooms more livable. Those details show how much work it took to keep a household going after a family had lost the freedom to choose where it lived.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Elisabeth Ruffner remembered helping people find references long after she became a volunteer adviser. In her 2007 interview she also described explaining the Hassayampa Hotel’s eligibility for the National Register to an owner.

Years earlier, Sharlot Hall had used her will to ask her successors to maintain and organize a collection and make it useful to the public. Her instructions and Ruffner’s memories show how much of preservation happens through records, conversations and years of patient work.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Sharlot Hall Museum campus preserves historic buildings. The operator sets which rooms are open.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: The Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community describes two distinct peoples, the Onk Akimel O’odham and the Xalychidom Piipaash. They share a government and have their own languages and cultures.
The museum building has a community history of its own. In a 2023 account, Museum Director Gary Owens described renovation work in the former Salt River Youth Home. The building went up in 1965–66.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Huhugam Ki: Museum’s public gallery is in the former youth home.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: In a 2015 statement about the documentary Ours Is the Land, Tohono O’odham Legislative Council member Art Wilson explained the duty to leave ancestors undisturbed. Elder Joseph Joaquin spoke about what a price on land leaves out.

The Nation’s own account describes longstanding ties to the Sonoran Desert and the way an international boundary divided lands and relationships. Both accounts can be read in the Nation’s published words.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: The first issue of Tubac’s Weekly Arizonian ran to four pages on March 3, 1859. Edward E. Cross was the editor, William Wrightson the publisher, and the Santa Rita Silver Mining Company owned it.

Cross had worked as a printer. The press is the part of his trade you can picture, but an editor also chose whose words would travel beyond town. The four pages survive in the Library of Congress catalog.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The public museum has a printing-history display. The record verifies the exhibit without promising a press demonstration.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Historian Lydia R. Otero grew up near Interstate 10 in Tucson and remembered how the freeway cut a working-class barrio off from the rest of the city. A separate redevelopment project, approved in 1966, targeted eighty acres of predominantly Mexican American downtown.

At La Casa Cordova, the Tucson Museum of Art tells the story of María Cordova, one of the residents displaced by urban renewal. A building could survive even when a family lost the chance to live there.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: Tucson’s Changing Landscape at La Casa Cordova connects North Meyer Avenue to the households and businesses that occupied it.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: David Lee helped his parents at Alan’s Market in Tucson’s Barrio Hollywood. He remembered whitewashing the building and painting the store sign himself. What might look like an uneven bit of lettering to a passerby was a child’s contribution to the family business.
The Tucson Chinese Cultural Center preserved Lee’s recollection. His account gives a name to work that can disappear behind the names of a store’s owners.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The center displays story boards about Tucson’s Chinese grocery stores.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Danette Bewley considered several aviation careers and chose airport management. She joined the Tucson Airport Authority in 2012. In a 2023 interview she credited mentors and the people she worked with along the way.
A museum airplane draws the eye to the pilot’s seat. Bewley’s account invites a visitor to notice the work done on the ground that a display aircraft alone cannot show.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Pima Air & Space Museum offers civilian aviation exhibits in its public museum.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: A 1936 photograph catalog record names two Harvey Girls at La Posada in Winslow, Ruby Gardner McHood and Myrtle Bass. Another worker, Verna Northcott Welsh, remembered hoping for a job at the hotel desk and ending up waiting tables.

Welsh preferred the two-to-ten shift. She had already left by the time Virginia Graff remembered wartime troop trains bringing crowds so large that even the familiar china and silver changed. These were two women remembering different working days.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Old Trails Museum occupies a former financial building dating to 1921. The museum opened there in 1989.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Joseph C. Ives’s 1861 report describes what it took to keep steam transport moving near Fort Yuma. People cut fuel wood, vessels waited for repairs, and a small settlement had a blacksmith’s shop.
Ives wrote as an observer. He named Captain Robinson and Mr. Carroll, but the workers themselves do not speak in those passages. Their work is visible in every delay and every load of fuel.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: At Register Rock, A. Freeman and D. Tickner signed their names in axle grease. Both left the same date, June 12, 1850. The marks preserve a day on the California Trail in material the travelers already had on their wagons.

Travelers saw different things among the same rocks. Sallie Hester thought they resembled ruined buildings. Margaret Frink preferred the name Pyramid City. Northern Shoshone and Bannock people knew this country long before either traveler arrived.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: From the Register Rock wayside, look for the names and dates on the rock. Camp Rock also carries inscriptions. The marks are fragile.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: In 1920, Robert Limbert and W. L. Cole spent seventeen days crossing about eighty miles of lava country with heavy gear and a camera. Limbert’s dog injured its feet on the broken lava. Photographs helped bring wider attention to a landscape that was already part of a living homeland.

A century later, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes and the National Park Service developed nine waysides at Devils Orchard. At the 2024 dedication, Nolan Brown described their purpose as showing visitors “who we are and where they are.”

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: The Robert Limbert Visitor Center houses the museum. The Devils Orchard waysides tell the Tribes’ connections to the lava country when that area is accessible.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Idaho City grew out of the Boise Basin gold rush in 1862. The town needed suppliers as much as it needed prospectors. Three early brick buildings on the mercantile block housed a succession of stores and a bank.

Researchers traced an 1873 sale of two lots, a house and a brick building to Wong Chong & Co. Later records connect Pon Yam with the business. The historical foundation describes it as both a supplier and a gathering place for Chinese residents.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: From public streets, look for the early brick commercial buildings and the old Pinney Post Office, now the Boise Basin Museum.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: At Three Island Crossing, emigrants faced a choice. They could try the Snake River for the northern route or stay on the south side and follow the Dry Route. The ford used two of the three islands on a route already known to Indigenous people and fur traders.

On August 9, 1845, Eli Casey Cooley recorded a wagon saved and part of its load lost. His party was still moving wagons and cattle the next morning. The account survives in a family transcription of his diary.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: From the overlook, the river divides around the islands. The old ford can be read from land.

sections.heading: Why this place matters
paragraphs: Nephi Rudolph “Cap” Hacken remembered selling popcorn and peanuts from a basket when Rudolph Valentino appeared at Saltair. Hacken put his age at about twelve and the visit around 1924 or 1925.

His account follows the work past the performance, into the cleaning up after visitors had gone home. His son Richard later edited the recollections and drawings. The first Saltair pavilion burned in 1925.
